los-angeles.intro: Los Angeles kept its old trees in odd places. A Little Tokyo parking lot holds the first living thing the city ever made a Historic-Cultural Monument, a hotel built its driveway around a fig, the oldest palm has been moved three times, and a fig in Pasadena has outlived the future mayor who planted it in his front yard in 1880. Ten of the nineteen here are Moreton Bay figs. They run from Santa Monica to Long Beach and Mission San Gabriel, so treat this as several trips, not one walk.
los-angeles.meta_description: Nineteen old trees of Los Angeles: a Little Tokyo fig made a city monument, a twice-lived oak at the Huntington, and a palm moved three times.
los-angeles.question_meta: A California fan palm in Exposition Park, in Los Angeles since the 1850s and moved three times, is the city's oldest documented tree.
los-angeles.question_answer: The oldest tree in Los Angeles is the palm in Exposition Park, a California fan palm documented in the city since the 1850s and already mature when it was first transplanted, which makes it at least 170 years old and probably more. It has been moved three times since. The runner-up is the olive in the garden of Mission San Gabriel, which the mission's own sign dates to the 1860s, about 160 years ago. Older by estimate, though not by any record, is a coast live oak in the Chinese Garden at The Huntington, which the Huntington itself puts at 200 to 300 years.
los-angeles.question_context: Almost nothing old in Los Angeles grew where it stands by accident, and many of the trees can be dated because someone wrote down what they planted. The olive at Mission San Gabriel goes back to the 1860s by the mission's sign. The figs followed: 1875 on the old plaza at El Pueblo and at St John's, around 1880 for the pair the Bixby family planted at Rancho Los Cerritos that later grew into one tree, 1880 for the fig Thomas Earley planted outside his Pasadena house, the 1890s for the matched pair at Rancho Los Alamitos, 1894 by the Automobile Club. Younger ones carry history too, like the Aoyama Tree, planted at a Little Tokyo temple in 1920. What Los Angeles lacks is a protected list of individual trees. The municipal code protects certain species rather than certain trees, which is why the city could lose the Encino Oak when it fell in 1998, and why a heritage sycamore in Griffith Park needed a lawsuit to stay standing. Single trees get protection one designation at a time, as Los Angeles gave the Aoyama Tree and Pasadena and South Pasadena gave their figs.

faq_add.q: What is the Aoyama Tree in Little Tokyo?
faq_add.a: A Moreton Bay fig planted in 1920 by the Reverend Shutai Aoyama at the entrance of a Buddhist temple. The temple is gone and the fig now stands in a parking lot north of the National Center for the Preservation of Democracy. In 2008 it became Historic-Cultural Monument No. 920, the first living thing on the city's list.

faq_add.q: Can I see the old figs at the Long Beach ranchos?
faq_add.a: Yes, both are free. Rancho Los Cerritos has a fig the Bixby family planted around 1880 as two trees that grew into one, and Rancho Los Alamitos has a matched pair from the 1890s. Both sites open Wednesday to Sunday with limited hours, so check before you drive.

faq_add.q: Is there an old tree at Mission San Gabriel?
faq_add.a: An olive in the mission garden, which the mission's sign says Father Bot planted in the 1860s, about 160 years ago. The garden charges a small admission, and the amount varies between listings.

faq_add.q: Which old trees can I see at The Huntington?
faq_add.a: Three are on this page: the Queensland kauri in the Rose Garden, a Montezuma cypress beside it grown from seed gathered in Mexico City in 1912, and the coast live oak in the Chinese Garden, which the Huntington puts at 200 to 300 years. The Huntington charges for entry.

san-diego.intro: San Diego's trees were planted, not inherited. In 1892 the city leased Kate Sessions park land on condition she plant a hundred trees a year in Balboa Park, and the 1915 exposition brought in much of the rest. The oldest anyone can date are around 130 to 150 years old. Eight trees stand in the city itself, from Balboa Park to Kensington; five more are across the bay in Coronado, a separate city with its own list of heritage trees, among them a Torrey pine named the city's Official Tree.
san-diego.meta_description: Thirteen old trees of San Diego and Coronado: a Guadalupe cypress from 1892, a hotel garden fig on Grape Street, and Coronado's official Torrey pine.
san-diego.question_meta: San Diego's oldest tree is a Guadalupe Island cypress in Balboa Park, planted around 1892 by Kate Sessions and now roughly 130 years old.
san-diego.question_answer: The oldest tree in San Diego is a Guadalupe Island cypress on the Sixth Avenue side of Balboa Park, beside the chess and horseshoe club building, at roughly 130 years. San Diego Magazine went looking for the city's oldest tree in 2020 and named this one, putting it at about 128 years then. It is one of the trees Kate Sessions planted under her 1892 lease of park land at Sixth and Upas, which obliged her to plant a hundred trees a year in Balboa Park.
san-diego.question_context:
A hundred and thirty years is a young answer by the standards of most cities, and here it is the right one. San Diego's shade was planted, mostly between 1892 and the 1915 Panama-California Exposition, so the oldest trees in the city are the earliest plantings rather than the last survivors of anything. The cypress is also unusual for its species, which grows wild only on Isla Guadalupe off Baja California. The runner-up is easier to date exactly. The Moreton Bay fig outside the Natural History Museum went in as a five-gallon sapling in 1914. The fig on the old Florence Hotel lot on Grape Street may be older than both; its sign says 1877, the city's record 1895.

Across the bay, Coronado tells the same story on a smaller scale. Its Torrey pines were planted about a century ago in a city-wide programme under its Parks Superintendent, Louis C. Bandel, by the city's account, though no planting year survives for any single one. The firmest planting date there belongs to the two Norfolk Island pines at the library, planted in 1909 for its opening, about 117 years ago.

faq_add.q: Which old trees can I see in Coronado?
faq_add.a: Five of the city's heritage trees on public ground: the Torrey pine in Palm Park that is Coronado's Official Tree, Torrey pines at the library and in Cronan Park, the library's two Norfolk Island pines from 1909, and the Norfolk Island pine in Rotary Plaza that serves as the town's Christmas tree.

faq_add.q: How do I get to the Coronado trees from San Diego?
faq_add.a: Take the ferry from the Broadway Pier to the Ferry Landing, or a bus over the Coronado Bridge, roughly 15 to 30 minutes; check the timetable. Palm Park is a short walk from the ferry, and the library and Rotary Plaza are on Orange Avenue. None of them needs a ticket.

faq_add.q: Is Coronado's Christmas tree a living tree?
faq_add.a: Yes. It is a Norfolk Island pine that Parks Superintendent Louis C. Bandel moved into Rotary Plaza in 1936 with money from the town's Rotarians, and it is lit each December.

faq_add.q: What is the Florence Hotel fig?
faq_add.a: A Moreton Bay fig on Grape Street in Bankers Hill, the last thing left of the Florence Hotel, which was torn down around 1948 to 1950. Its sign says 1877 and the city's landmark record 1895. It has been Historical Site No. 53 since 1971 and stands on private ground, so look from the sidewalk.

faq_replace.Are San Diego's remarkable trees free to: Yes, every one. Five stand in Balboa Park with no ticket and no gate, though Marston House itself charges for tours inside; one is on a street corner in Pacific Beach beside its historical landmark plaque; the Kensington hoop pine is in a public park; the Florence Hotel fig is on private ground and seen from the sidewalk; the Coronado trees stand in parks, at the library and on street corners.

oakland.intro: Oakland has one old-growth coast redwood left, Old Survivor, about 470 years old by a 1969 ring count, on a cliff in Leona Heights Park that you see from the road. Downtown, in front of City Hall, stands the oak the city moved there in 1917 to honour Jack London. This page also crosses into Berkeley for two trees on the UC campus: a blue gum grove the university thinks is the tallest stand of hardwoods in North America, and a buckeye a 1950s committee wanted cut down.
oakland.meta_description: Oakland's old trees: Old Survivor, its last old-growth redwood, the Jack London Oak at City Hall, and the blue gum grove on the Berkeley campus.
oakland.question_meta: Oakland's oldest tree is Old Survivor, its last old-growth coast redwood, dated by a 1969 ring count to about 470 years.
oakland.question_answer: The oldest tree in Oakland is Old Survivor, the city's last old-growth coast redwood, in Leona Heights Park. A 1969 core sample counted 415 to 420 rings, which makes it about 470 years old today; some coverage says nearly 500. It is an Oakland Designated Landmark, and you see it from the sidewalk on Campus Drive, since there is no trail to the trunk.
oakland.question_context:
Old Survivor grows on a steep rocky cliff among younger second-growth redwoods, and its exact spot is deliberately not published, to protect the habitat around it. That is why our pin sits on Campus Drive, opposite Carl B. Munck Elementary School, where you can look across at it, rather than on the tree. The York Trail gives a more distant view. Please keep off the school grounds.

The other three trees are easier. The Jack London Oak stands in Frank H. Ogawa Plaza in front of City Hall, three minutes from 12th Street City Center BART. It came from Mosswood Park in 1917, already about twenty, which puts it somewhere between 120 and 160 years old; the plaza holds other oaks, so look for its 2017 plaque.

In Berkeley, both campus trees are on open university grounds a short walk from Downtown Berkeley BART. The blue gum grove on Strawberry Creek was planted in 1877 or 1882, depending on which university page you read, as a windbreak for a running track. The buckeye in Faculty Glade was already standing in the 1950s; its real age is not documented.

faq.q: Can I walk to Old Survivor?
faq.a: No. There is no trail to the trunk and its exact location is kept unpublished to protect the habitat. You see it from the sidewalk on Campus Drive, across from Carl B. Munck Elementary School, or at a distance from the York Trail.

faq.q: Why is there a Jack London Oak at Oakland City Hall?
faq.a: The city moved a coast live oak from Mosswood Park to City Hall in 1917 to honour Jack London, who had died the year before. Its original plaque went missing for decades, and it was re-dedicated with a new one in 2017.

faq.q: Are the UC Berkeley trees open to visitors?
faq.a: Yes. The eucalyptus grove on Strawberry Creek and the buckeye in Faculty Glade are on open campus grounds, free and with no posted hours, about five to twelve minutes on foot from Downtown Berkeley BART.

faq.q: How old is the eucalyptus grove at Berkeley?
faq.a: Roughly 145 years. One university page says it was planted in 1882 as a windbreak for the old cinder track; a 2010 university news story says 1877.

glen-ellen.intro: Two trees in Jack London State Historic Park, above the village of Glen Ellen. Jack's Oak, a coast live oak put at nearly 400 years, spreads beside the cottage where Jack and Charmian London lived, and it was nearly felled in 2013 before tests gave it more time. A walk of about 3.5 miles there and back reaches the Grandmother Tree, a redwood the park estimates at 1,800 to 2,000 years, a survivor of the giants that once surrounded Glen Ellen.
glen-ellen.meta_description: Two old trees in Jack London State Historic Park, Glen Ellen: the Grandmother Tree, a redwood of up to 2,000 years, and Jack's Oak by the cottage.
glen-ellen.question_meta: Glen Ellen's oldest tree is the Grandmother Tree, a coast redwood in Jack London State Historic Park estimated at 1,800 to 2,000 years.
glen-ellen.question_answer: The oldest tree in Glen Ellen is the Grandmother Tree, a coast redwood on the Ancient Redwood Trail in Jack London State Historic Park. The park estimates it at 1,800 to 2,000 years; that is its estimate, not a ring count. It is about a 3.5 mile round trip on foot from the park, with a climb of around 200 feet.
glen-ellen.question_context:
Both trees are inside Jack London State Historic Park, which California State Parks runs with Jack London Park Partners. The park opens daily from 9 to 5. Day use is listed at $10 a car on its fees page, with $15 reported from June 2026, so check. There is no public transport to the gate; it is about five minutes by car from Glen Ellen village and twenty from Sonoma.

Jack's Oak is the easy one, a short walk from the Beauty Ranch car park, beside the London Cottage. London bought his first parcels here in 1905. The oak is old and weakened by fungus, and the newest sighting we have is from February 2025, so tell us how it looks if you go. A seedling from its acorns grows beside it.

The Grandmother Tree takes the afternoon. From the Lake, take the Vineyard Trail, cross Asbury Creek, and at the three-way junction with the Fern Lake Trail follow the small centre path past a picnic table and hitching posts. The park gives it a diameter of about 14 feet, though others say 14 feet around. Dogs are not allowed on the back-country trails.

faq.q: How old is the Grandmother Tree?
faq.a: The park estimates 1,800 to 2,000 years. It is an estimate rather than a ring count, so read it as a range.

faq.q: How long is the walk to the Grandmother Tree?
faq.a: About 3.5 miles there and back, moderate, with a climb of around 200 feet, on the Ancient Redwood Trail. Dogs are not allowed on the back-country trails.

As of a visitor's record from February 2025, yes. It was weakened by fungal infection and nearly removed in 2013, but tests showed it could stand a while longer, and a seedling from its acorns was planted beside it.

sebastopol.intro: Sebastopol keeps what is left of Luther Burbank's Gold Ridge Experiment Farm, a three-acre remnant saved in the 1970s. Its oldest tree is a Royal Hybrid Black Walnut that Burbank planted in 1885, the year he bought the land, as a witness tree on the property line. It is stop number one on the farm's self-guided tour, free from dawn to dusk.
sebastopol.meta_description: Luther Burbank's Royal walnut, planted in 1885 as a boundary marker on his Gold Ridge Experiment Farm in Sebastopol, free to visit daily.
sebastopol.question_meta: Sebastopol's oldest mapped tree is Luther Burbank's Royal Hybrid Black Walnut, planted in 1885 on his Gold Ridge Experiment Farm.
sebastopol.question_answer: The oldest tree we map in Sebastopol is the Royal Hybrid Black Walnut on Luther Burbank's Gold Ridge Experiment Farm, planted in 1885, about 140 years ago. The historical society that runs the farm calls it the oldest tree on the grounds; it went in as a witness tree marking the property line, and Burbank introduced the Royal walnut in 1893.
sebastopol.question_context: Burbank bought this land in 1885, and what survives is a three-acre remnant the Society saved in the 1970s. The farm is run by the Western Sonoma County Historical Society on land owned by the City of Sebastopol, about a mile's walk west of Main Street. It is free and open daily from dawn to dusk, with docent tours by appointment for a small fee. The walnut is stop number one on the Society's self-guided tour, and other original Burbank plantings follow along the route, including a hybrid chestnut and a Paradox walnut. The Royal is a cross between the California black walnut and an eastern walnut, and a Society member has said it once produced a ton of nuts in a season. Nobody has published its height or girth, and the newest evidence that it stands is the Society's current tour rather than a dated photograph, so tell us how it looks if you visit.

faq.q: Is the Luther Burbank Experiment Farm free?
faq.a: Yes, open daily from dawn to dusk. Docent tours are by appointment for a small fee.
A tree planted or kept to mark a property line. The Society says Burbank's Royal walnut went in for that purpose in 1885.
On Bodega Avenue in Sebastopol, about a mile's walk west of Main Street. The walnut is the first stop on the self-guided tour.

santa-barbara.intro: Santa Barbara's oldest trees are its first plantings, and the biggest of them came off a ship. A sailor brought a Moreton Bay fig from Australia in 1876; it now stands beside the train station with a crown more than 175 feet across. Four of the five trees here are downtown within about a mile and a half: the fig, a pepper tree older than City Hall, five lemon-scented gums at the library and a dragon tree in Alameda Park. The fifth, a dragon tree from an 1890s nursery, is at Lotusland in Montecito, by booked tour only.
santa-barbara.meta_description: Five old trees of Santa Barbara: the 1876 Moreton Bay fig by the station, City Hall's pepper tree, the library gums and two dragon trees.
santa-barbara.question_meta: Santa Barbara's oldest tree is the Moreton Bay fig at Chapala and Montecito Streets, planted in 1876 or 1877, about 150 years ago.
santa-barbara.question_answer: The oldest dated tree in Santa Barbara is the Moreton Bay fig at the corner of Chapala and Montecito Streets, beside the Amtrak station. A sailor brought it from Australia as a seedling in 1876 and it was planted on this corner in 1876 or 1877, so it is about 150 years old. Its trunk is about 45 feet around by the city's measure. The runner-up is the oldest dragon tree at Lotusland in Montecito, which the garden traces to an 1890s nursery.
santa-barbara.question_context:
Santa Barbara may have older trees than its oldest dated one, but not with dates. The pepper tree in front of City Hall was already fully grown in a photograph from about 1924, when the building went up beside it, and nobody wrote down when it was planted, so it may be as old as the fig or older. The city made the building and the tree one landmark in 2000.

The fig is the one with a record. It came from Australia as a seedling in 1876 and went into this corner in 1876 or 1877, depending on whether you follow the city or the local tree group Santa Barbara Beautiful, which credits Adeline Crabb with the planting. It became a city landmark in 1970 and its ground was deeded to the city in 1976.

The dragon trees are the town's other speciality. Santa Barbara Beautiful names the two largest in California as late-1800s trees in private gardens. Of the ones a visitor can reach, the oldest dated is at Lotusland, from Kinton Stevens' nursery of the 1890s, and Alameda Park has a mature one nobody has dated.

faq.q: Where is the Moreton Bay fig in Santa Barbara?
faq.a: At the corner of Chapala and West Montecito Streets, beside the Amtrak station, in a small city park named after it. It is free. A barrier keeps visitors off the roots, so you see it from the paths around the edge.

faq.q: Can I walk between Santa Barbara's old trees?
faq.a: Four of them, yes. The fig by the station, the pepper tree in front of City Hall, the five lemon-scented gums at the Central Library and the dragon tree in Alameda Park are all within about a mile and a half, and all are free.

faq.q: Can I see the old dragon tree at Lotusland?
faq.a: Only on a guided tour booked in advance. Lotusland is in a residential part of Montecito, tours run mostly from mid-February to mid-November, Wednesday to Saturday, and dates sell out. The oldest dragon tree there traces to an 1890s nursery.

faq.q: Are Santa Barbara's landmark trees free to visit?
faq.a: Four of the five are: a city park, a public plaza, the library grounds and Alameda Park. Lotusland charges for its booked tours.

san-jose.intro: San Jose's oldest trees go back to the mission and the first adobes. Behind the Roberto Adobe in Willow Glen grows a fig the city lists as one of the oldest in Santa Clara County, planted some time between 1847 and 1881. Next door in Santa Clara, the olives by the Adobe Wall at Santa Clara University were probably planted between 1822 and 1825, when the ground belonged to the Mission Santa Clara de Asís. Both are free; the fig only on the museum's open Saturdays.
san-jose.meta_description: Two old trees of San Jose and Santa Clara: mission olives from the 1820s and a heritage fig behind the Roberto Adobe.
san-jose.question_meta: The oldest trees near San Jose are the mission olives at Santa Clara University, probably planted between 1822 and 1825.
san-jose.question_answer: The oldest dated trees in the San Jose area are the olives along the Adobe Wall at Santa Clara University, which the university's archive says were probably planted between 1822 and 1825, when the land belonged to the Mission Santa Clara de Asís. In San Jose itself, the fig behind the Roberto Adobe on Lincoln Avenue is on the city's heritage tree list as one of the oldest fig trees in Santa Clara County.
san-jose.question_context:
San Jose protects its old trees one at a time. The city keeps a heritage tree list, adopted by council resolution with a number and a measurement for each tree, and the fig behind the Roberto Adobe is HT-03-012 on it, with a trunk about 38 inches across and a note calling it one of the oldest fig trees in the county. Its planting date is lost. A local account puts it between 1847, when the Suñol family's brick house went up beside the adobe, and 1881.

The mission is older still. The olive trees along the Adobe Wall at Santa Clara University were probably planted between 1822 and 1825, by the university archive's account, and the wall and the Adobe Lodge beside them are the oldest structures on the campus. Nobody has counted how many of the first olives survive, and the archive says only that many still stand. Santa Clara is its own city, about fifteen minutes from downtown San Jose by Caltrain or bus.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in San Jose?
faq.a: The city's heritage list calls the fig behind the Roberto Adobe on Lincoln Avenue one of the oldest fig trees in Santa Clara County, planted some time between 1847 and 1881. The mission olives in neighbouring Santa Clara are older, from about 1822 to 1825.

faq.q: When can I see the Roberto Adobe fig?
faq.a: When the museum is open, the first and third Saturdays of the month from 1 to 3 pm by its own page. Entry is free; check before you go, as hours have changed over the years.

faq.q: Are the Santa Clara mission olives open to visitors?
faq.a: Yes. They grow along the Adobe Wall in the Mission Gardens behind the Mission Church, on the open Santa Clara University campus, and we found no fee.
